# Where 35.5 Comes From

## The Simple Average Does Not Work

The obvious thing to try is the simple average of the two isotopes: (35 + 37) ÷ 2 = 36 u. That is not the 35.5 u in the table. A simple average treats both isotopes as equally common, and they are not. In nature there are about 3 atoms of chlorine-35 for every 1 atom of chlorine-37.

<!-- STEP id="weighted" -->
## Count Every Atom

Take four chlorine atoms, mixed as they are in nature: three of 35 u and one of 37 u. Their total mass is 105 + 37 = 142 u, so the average is 142 ÷ 4 = **35.5 u**.

The same sum with percentages uses 75% and 25%: (35 × 75/100) + (37 × 25/100) = 35.5 u. This is called the **weighted average atomic mass**, because each isotope counts according to how common it is.

Try it: change the mix and see where the average lands.

<!-- STEP id="lakh" -->
## Ten Lakh Atoms

This does not mean that any chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5 u. Take 10 lakh chlorine atoms: 7.5 lakh of them have a mass of 35 u and 2.5 lakh have a mass of 37 u. Not one atom has 35.5 u, but that is the average of all of them.

<!-- STEP id="takeaway" -->
## What the Table Tells You

If you predicted an average, you were right. Half a neutron does not exist, and 17 electrons are far too light to add 0.5 u.

**The atomic mass of an element is a weighted average of its isotopes, not the mass of any one atom.**
